lecture_metadata.title: But what is a neural network? (3Blue1Brown)

chunk_summaries: john avlon shows you what a neural network actually is, assuming no background . avlon: this video is going to be devoted to the structure component of a neural network . avlon: we're going to put together a video to show you what a neural network actually is .

a neural network can learn to recognize handwritten digits . it's a pretty cool thing for a computer to be able to do . the code that does this can be downloaded and played with on your own computer .
784 neurons make up the first layer of our network . each neuron is lit up when its activation is a high number . the network has already been trained to recognize digits .

sally kohn: the network has already been trained to recognize digits . kohn: it's reasonable to expect a layered structure like this to behave intelligently . she says a 9 has a loop up top, an 8 has a line on the right, an 8 has a line down low . kohn: we might hope that any generally loopy pattern towards the top sets off this neuron .

bob greene: learning which subcomponents correspond to which digits is tricky . he says recognizing a loop can also break down into subproblems . greene: it's a hope that we might have, a sort of goal with the layered structure . he says it could be useful for other image recognition tasks .

the goal is to have some mechanism that could conceivably combine pixels into edges . john sutter: we'll assign a weight to each one of the connections between neurons . he says we'll use green pixels to indicate positive weights, red pixels to indicate negative weights . sutter: the goal is to have some mechanism that could conceivably combine pixels into edges .

weighted sum of all pixel values adds up values of the pixel just in the region that we care about . the sum is largest when those middle pixels are bright but the surrounding pixels are darker . neuron activation is a measure of how positive the relevant weighted sum is . but maybe you only want it to be active when the sum is bigger than 10 .

the network has almost exactly exactly 13,000 total weights and biases . the network can be tweaked and turned to make it behave in different ways . if you tweak the numbers by hand, you have a starting place .

the weighted sum of the activations in the first layer corresponds to one of the terms in the matrix vector product of everything we have on the left . instead of talking about adding the bias to each one of these values independently, we represent it by organizing all those biases into a vector, and adding the entire vector to the previous matrix vector product .

the sigmoid function is a function that takes in 784 numbers as an input and spits out 10 numbers as an output . the entire network is just a function, one that takes in 784 numbers as an input and spits out 10 numbers as an output . it's an absurdly complicated function that involves 13,000 parameters in the form of weights and biases .

cnn's nina dos santos looks at the neural networks that underlie YouTube's recommendation algorithm . santos: we should quickly bring up this sigmoid function . she says relatively few modern networks actually use sigmoid anymore . dos santos: sigmoid is a very powerful neural network .

if it passes a certain threshold it would be the identity function . but if it did not then it would just not be activated so it'd be zero . people just tried ReLU and it happened to work very well for these incredibly deep neural networks .

lecture_metadata.title: Neoliberalism and the End of History - Part 3

chunk_summaries: racism grew partly out of the Enlightenment, says noam chomsky . as the age of exploration continued, Europeans were finding creatures of a kind that they had never seen before, like orangutans .

neoliberal policies of the last generation have undermined a large part of the population . for a majority of the population, conditions have stagnated or declined during the period that began with Reagan . in 2007, there was great euphoria among economists and intellectuals about the wonderful economy .

arlie hochschild: the people who are suffering the most from neoliberal policies are the ones who most support them . she says the more he kicks them in the face at every opportunity, the more they support him . hochschild: neoliberal policies aren't working, they're a threat to the working class . she says it's a paradox that the people who are suffering the most are those who support them .

bob greene: people behind us are being pushed by the federal government in front of us . he says the problem is the people behind us, who don't want to work, who are worthless . greene: they're saturated with talk radio, talk about welfare queens driving to welfare office . greene: we've got to stop putting people behind us in front of us with affirmative action programs .

john avlon: people behind us are being pushed by the federal government . avlon: we're stalled, but it's not because of those people behind us . avlon: it's going to be necessary to turn their attention to somebody who's doing that to them . avlon: we're going to see more of what's going to happen unless there's strong reaction .

race riots back in our own history are often like this, says michael degraff . degraff: everywhere you look, you find one or another aspect of it . gynecology was developed by professors at Harvard medical school, he says . degraff: if you shoot any creole phonemic pattern in your french, you're discarded .

linguist: race alongside language can create illusion of hierarchies . linguist: if you speak in french, you're discarded by the jury . linguist: if you speak in black english, you're discarded by the jury . linguist: if you speak in black english, you're discarded by the jury .

the picking up of a fake acc-- it shows up in many strange ways . people-- men, of course. no women-- dressed in English clothes and affected British accents . but these things happen all the time when it's a part of the population .

lecture_metadata.title: Why Having More Doesn't Make You Happier (Science of Well-Being)

chunk_summaries: our minds just don't think in terms of absolutes . instead, we think in terms of a reference point . the ebinghouse illusion is a really cool illusion in vision .

bob greene: we're constantly judging relative to other stuff out there in the world . greene: is it really the case that we judge the kinds of events that happen in our lives . he asks: is Michael Phelps a relevant reference point for other people's happiness? greene: we're constantly judging relative to other stuff out there in the world .
lazlo C, or Chay. Lazloch, is not looking very happy at all . bronze winner is Ryan Lock Day from back in the day . but he's actually looking really, really smiley than the silver medal winner .

cnn's john avlon says the silver medal winners are less happy than the bronze . avlon: it's not your absolute level or the absolute medal you got. it's what you think you could have gotten . avlon: if you're a bronze medal winner, what's your most salient reference point?

many of us aren't going to have reference points that are that salient like the gold medal in the 200 meter . most of our evaluation of what a good job is actually concerns having a high salary . what we used to make in terms of our salary is a pretty salient reference point .

aaron carroll: we're constantly bumping ourselves up when we think of a good income . carroll: for every amount that your actual income goes up a dollar, your required income goes up a $140 . he says we're constantly below the reference point we seek; it's our social comparisons . carroll: we're constantly below the reference point we seek; we're constantly below the reference point .

psychologists say we care a lot about where we stand relative to other people . comparisons against other people are one of the number one things that affect our job satisfaction . if you feel like you're making less, you like your job even less .

bob greene: if you're in a job where your co-workers have a higher salary than you, you're less happy . greene: it makes you so unhappy that humans do what they tend to do when they're unhappy . he says over 50% of people choose having half of the income so they won't be less than others . greene: if you're in a job where your co-workers have a higher salary than you, you're less happy

study: unemployed are worse off when they're unemployed than when they're employed . study: if you're unemployed in a spot where lots of other people are unemployed, you're fine . if you're unemployed in a spot where lots of other people are unemployed, it's not as bad .

we're so prone to social comparisons that even something like not having a job depends on it . john sutter: we treat others who are employed or in your zip code as being a reasonable social comparison . he says our minds seem to soak in anything around us as a reference point . sutter: if we compare ourselves to beyonce, we're taking in references that are crazy .

the more TV you watch, the more unhappy you are with your own income . for every hour of extra TV watching you do a week you are spending $4 more a week . the more you watch, the more unhappy you are with your own income .

for every hour of extra TV you watch a week, people are spending $4 more each week . peggy drexler: we're not calculating who's really a good reference point to be near . drexler: do you try to keep up with people in your neighborhood who have won the lottery? she says if you live close to someone with a prominent new car in their garage, does that mess with you? drexler: we're just trying to keep up with

lottery winners are almost twice as likely to buy a new car if they live next to a person who won the lottery . ruben navarrette: it's a really insidious reference point . navarrette: it's like whoever we happen to be near and whatever lives we happen to see . navarrette: if you're in a control case, you're almost twice as likely to buy a new car yourself .

a study shows that as other people's grades go up, your unhappiness with your own grades are going down . lz granderson: that can lead to these insidious spiteful behaviors about other people's grades . he says if you check this off, you're going to get 0.567% on your final grade point average . granderson: if you're at 69.0 and you go to 69.5, you know, we round up .
about 41% of students rejected the proposal to do this . ruben navarrette: the rejections were higher in the top 50% of the class . navarrette: the class as a whole approves of this policy .

ruben navarrette: rejections were higher in the top 50% of the class . navarrette: this is a spot that's super insidious . he says students are willing to miss out on their own grade bonus because of this . navarrette: if you're like me, you're constantly faced with these social comparisons .

ruben navarrette: a few minutes of looking at pictures makes you more unhappy . navarrette: it's true of your own perceptions of yourself, but can this mess up others? he says social comparisons mess up our perceptions of other people . navarrette: if you're tracking, it's messing up all the stuff we talked about .

a study looked at how much looking at your social comparisons improves or messes up your self-esteem . there's a pretty high correlation between Facebook use and self-esteem, the study found . the study also looked at the direction of your comparisons .

there's twice as big a correlation between Facebook use and self-esteem . a new study found that the more Facebook use you have, the lower your self-esteem . the study also found that if you're making downward comparisons, your self-esteem is about that .

rated self-esteem is about that, but it's much lower than if you're doing upward comparisons . you get a little bump when you're making downward comparisons, but not very much . all the data suggests that across social media, all these problems with reference points are kicking in .

the more you can force that filter on it, the better you will be . the more you can force that filter on it, the better you will be . the more you can force that filter on it, the better you will be .
